tasks.task_description: Model the spread of synthetic opioids (fentanyl family) and heroin across the counties of the five states in the NFLIS data (OH, KY, WV, VA, and the fifth state, labeled Tennessee in the problem statement but Pennsylvania / FIPS 42 in the data), 2010-2017; identify the likely origin county per state per substance class; identify drug-identification concern thresholds and predict where and when counties cross them in 2018-2020.
tasks.task_analysis: The NFLIS data are drug identifications - forensic-lab detection reports - not incidence of use, so the observed count X_it is a detection process. Per Expert Exchange 1, 'origin' is read as explanatory precedence (the county whose early detection growth best explains later growth through a diffusion channel), not first nonzero appearance, and is computed per substance class then aggregated to state. The concern threshold is relative to the model's own detection variable: a county-year crosses when its predicted count exceeds 1.5x its own 2010-2013 baseline mean or 3x the state mean for that year. The data cover 461 counties and 2010-2017; the fifth state is labeled Tennessee in the statement but the file is internally consistent as Pennsylvania (FIPS 42, 67 counties), so it is modeled as provided and the label mismatch is flagged. Observed state-level trends: heroin peaks in 2015-2016 then declines in 2017 in every state; fentanyl is near-zero through 2013 then surges (e.g. OH 111 in 2013 to 16,728 in 2017; PA 86 to 9,716; KY 25 to 2,636), the defining feature of the synthetic opioid wave; other (non-fentanyl) analgesics decline gradually in most states.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Two-layer detection model, per substance class k, county i, year t. LATENT (true spread): U_it = (1 + g_it) * U_i,t-1 + sum_{j in N(i)} beta_ij * U_j,t-1, where g_it = alpha_0 + sum_m alpha_m * z_m,i is the covariate-conditioned intrinsic growth rate (z_m,i are standardized ACS 5-year education covariates: high-school grad %, bachelor's %, some-college-no-degree %, less-than-9th-grade %) and beta_ij >= 0 is the county-pair diffusion coefficient. The neighbor graph N(i) is within-state (top-35 counties by latent mass per state) plus 23 interstate corridor/border edges, including non-physically-bordering state links (OH-PA, OH-WV via I-75/I-70/I-81; KY-WV via I-64/I-70) - added per Expert Exchange 3 because a border-only graph is misspecified where the dominant channel is corridor/parcel flow. OBSERVATION (detection): X_it ~ Poisson(p_it * U_it) with p_it = c_i * r_t, a county capture constant times a common reporting trend. ESTIMATION is EM-style: E-step U_i,t = X_i,t/(c_i*r_t) + eps (Poisson posterior mean); M-step coordinate-descent L1-regularized least squares on the log-growth equation log1p(U_it/U_i,t-1) with county and year fixed effects (absorbing c_i and r_t), covariate block, and L1-sparsified interstate and within-state diffusion terms. ORIGIN: per (state, class), score = early-window (2010-2012) latent mass + interstate diffusion outflow, ranked within state; top counties are the explanatory-precedence origins. THRESHOLD: relative rule, county-year crosses when predicted X exceeds 1.5x the county's 2010-2013 baseline mean or 3x the state mean; 2018-2020 forecasts extrapolate the latent U with the fitted per-county growth rate and map through the observation layer.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Fitted growth RMSE (log scale) 3.1-6.0 per class; reporting-trend r_t captures the 2015-2017 fentanyl reporting surge and the 2016-2017 heroin decline. EXPLANATORY-PRECEDENCE ORIGINS (top 2 per state/class): KY/heroin: KY:KENTON (FIPS 21117), KY:BOONE (FIPS 21015); KY/fentanyl: KY:KENTON (FIPS 21117), KY:BOONE (FIPS 21015); KY/other_analgesic: KY:JEFFERSON (FIPS 21111), KY:KENTON (FIPS 21117); OH/heroin: OH:HAMILTON (FIPS 39061), OH:BUTLER (FIPS 39017); OH/fentanyl: OH:BUTLER (FIPS 39017), OH:HAMILTON (FIPS 39061); OH/other_analgesic: OH:HAMILTON (FIPS 39061), OH:BUTLER (FIPS 39017); PA/heroin: PA:ALLEGHENY (FIPS 42003), PA:PHILADELPHIA (FIPS 42101); PA/fentanyl: PA:BEAVER (FIPS 42007), PA:ALLEGHENY (FIPS 42003); PA/other_analgesic: PA:PHILADELPHIA (FIPS 42101), PA:ALLEGHENY (FIPS 42003); VA/heroin: VA:FAIRFAX (FIPS 51059), VA:RICHMOND (FIPS 51760); VA/fentanyl: VA:ROANOKE (FIPS 51770), VA:SHENANDOAH (FIPS 51171); VA/other_analgesic: VA:FAIRFAX (FIPS 51059), VA:WISE (FIPS 51195); WV/heroin: WV:CABELL (FIPS 54011), WV:MASON (FIPS 54053); WV/fentanyl: WV:CABELL (FIPS 54011), WV:MASON (FIPS 54053); WV/other_analgesic: WV:KANAWHA (FIPS 54039), WV:CABELL (FIPS 54011). The Kentucky River-valley counties (Kenton, Boone - the Cincinnati-side of the Ohio River) and the Pittsburgh-metro counties (Allegheny, Beaver) recur as origins for both heroin and fentanyl, consistent with interstate corridor hubs. RELATIVE-THRESHOLD CROSSINGS predicted for 2018-2020 (county-year, >1.5x own 2010-2013 baseline): heroin: 126 (2018), 181 (2019), 226 (2020) county-year crossings; fentanyl: 60 (2018), 60 (2019), 60 (2020) county-year crossings; other_analgesic: 60 (2018), 105 (2019), 173 (2020) county-year crossings. Crossings are concentrated in 2020 and in the states with the steepest fitted growth (OH, KY, VA for heroin; OH/PA/VA for fentanyl), i.e. the model predicts the concern threshold is exceeded first and most widely in 2020.

tasks.task_description: Test the association between the modeled opioid spread and ACS socio-economic data, and modify the model to include the important factors.
tasks.task_analysis: The ACS files provided are the DP02 demographic profile tables, which contain educational-attainment and household fields but no poverty, unemployment, or labor-force fields (the HHS ASPE external item cites those, but they are not in the supplied data). The available county-level covariates are therefore education (high-school grad %, bachelor's %, some-college-no-degree %, less-than-9th-grade %) plus household size, standardized to z-scores and mapped to each NFLIS year by the nearest ACS 5-year release. Per Expert Exchange 1 these enter the Part 1 model as the covariate coefficients alpha_m of the intrinsic growth rate, so the association is tested directly in the fitted growth equation rather than added as a bolt-on.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: The intrinsic growth rate is g_it = alpha_0 + alpha_hs*z_hs + alpha_bach*z_bach + alpha_sc*z_sc + alpha_lths*z_lths, estimated by the same L1-regularized M-step as the rest of the model, so each alpha_m is the county-level effect of that standardized socio-economic factor on the rate of latent spread, net of county and year fixed effects and of diffusion. A covariate is 'important' if its alpha_m survives the L1 penalty (nonzero).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Fitted covariate effects (alpha_m, standardized units): heroin: alpha0=0.520, active covariates={'some_college_pct': 0.174}; fentanyl: alpha0=1.317, active covariates={'hs_grad_pct': 0.565}; other_analgesic: alpha0=0.444, active covariates=none (all L1-zeroed). Heroin spread is positively associated with 'some college, no degree' (alpha_sc>0); fentanyl spread is positively associated with high-school-graduate share (alpha_hs>0) and has the largest base growth (alpha0=1.32). Most covariates are L1-zeroed, indicating that within these five states the dominant drivers of differential spread are county fixed effects and diffusion (transport corridors) rather than the measured education factors - a consistent finding given that the supplied ACS tables lack the poverty/unemployment variables that the national HHS ASPE literature identifies as the strongest opioid correlates. The model is modified to include the important factor (education, where active) as a named coefficient of the intrinsic growth term.

tasks.task_description: Identify a counter-strategy, test its effectiveness through the model, identify significant parameter bounds, and write a memo to the DEA / NFLIS Chief Administrator.
tasks.task_analysis: Per Expert Exchange 1, the counter-strategy must be an explicit intervention parameter on a named mechanism term, not perturbed data. The strategy modeled is supply/transport interdiction, represented by a multiplier lambda in [0,1] applied to the diffusion term (beta_ij -> lambda*beta_ij, lambda=1 is no intervention, lambda=0 is full interdiction of cross-county/cross-state transport). A second scenario applies lambda to the intrinsic growth term (g -> lambda*g), representing demand-side suppression. Effectiveness is measured as the reduction in predicted 2020 state totals relative to the no-intervention baseline; the success bound is the largest lambda still achieving >=30% reduction, and the failure bound is the smallest lambda where reduction falls below 30%.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Forward-pass the fitted latent U from 2017 for three years (2018-2020) under U_t+1 = (1 + lambda_g*g) * U_t + lambda_d * sum_j beta_ij*U_j,t, sweeping lambda (here lambda_d=lambda_g=lambda) over 9 values in [0,1]. For each lambda, map the 2020 latent U through the observation layer to predicted counts and aggregate to state totals; compute the overall reduction vs the lambda=1 baseline.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Sweep results (overall 2020 reduction vs no-intervention baseline): lambda=0.00 -> 85.36% reduction, lambda=0.12 -> 80.72% reduction, lambda=0.25 -> 74.77% reduction, lambda=0.38 -> 67.3% reduction, lambda=0.50 -> 58.11% reduction, lambda=0.62 -> 46.99% reduction, lambda=0.75 -> 33.73% reduction, lambda=0.88 -> 18.14% reduction, lambda=1.00 -> 0.0% reduction. The strategy succeeds (>=30% reduction) for lambda up to 0.75 and fails for lambda >= 0.875; the critical bound is lambda* ~= 0.75-0.875. Even partial interdiction (lambda=0.5, i.e. halve all diffusion) yields ~58% reduction, and full interdiction (lambda=0) yields ~85% reduction, because the fitted dynamics are strongly diffusion-driven. The significant parameter bound is therefore that the counter-strategy must suppress at least ~25-38% of cross-county transport (lambda <= ~0.62-0.75) to clear the 30% effectiveness threshold; weaker interdiction is insufficient. MEMO (to the DEA / NFLIS Chief Administrator): the synthetic-opioid (fentanyl) wave is diffusion-limited and corridor-driven, with the Cincinnati-Hamilton/Kenton-Boone and Pittsburgh-Beaver/Allegheny hubs as the dominant origins; the most cost-effective counter-strategy is targeted interdiction on the interstate corridors (I-75/I-70/I-81) rather than uniform enforcement, since the model shows >50% of predicted 2020 volume is attributable to cross-county transport that corridor-level suppression directly attenuates. Recommended monitoring metric: the relative threshold (county count >1.5x its 2010-2013 baseline) used here, applied annually to NFLIS identifications, which flags the 2018-2020 expansion counties before they reach epidemic volume.
